content: Managing serious bacterial infections in young infants aged 0–59 days is critical, especially in settings where referral to a hospital is not feasible. Infections account for approximately one-fifth of neonatal deaths globally, with sepsis, meningitis, and pneumonia being significant contributors. Prompt identification and treatment of young infants showing signs of possible serious bacterial infection (PSBI) are essential to reduce mortality and morbidity. A new guideline developed by WHO and UNICEF provides simplified antibiotic regimens for treating sick young infants in resource-limited settings where families cannot access or do not accept referral care. This guideline aims to increase access to treatment and adherence, ultimately saving lives. Ministries of health, international organizations, and pediatric associations play a vital role in supporting the introduction and adaptation of these guidelines into national policies and practices. Home visits during the first week after birth are recommended to counsel families, identify danger signs, and promote care-seeking behavior. These visits can be conducted by clinicians, midwives, or trained community health workers (CHWs). However, in many high-mortality settings, hospitalization and life-saving treatment may not be accessible, acceptable, or affordable for families. Studies in South Asia and Africa indicate that up to two-thirds or more of families refuse hospital referral for young infants with PSBI. The new WHO guideline addresses care for young infants in outpatient settings when referral is not feasible. It emphasizes the role of trained health workers in managing PSBI using simplified treatment regimens. For example, infants aged 7–59 days with fast breathing as the only sign of illness can be treated with oral amoxicillin twice daily for seven days without requiring hospitalization. For infants aged 0–6 days with fast breathing, referral to a hospital is recommended after pre-referral treatment. If referral is refused, oral amoxicillin can be administered by a trained health worker. For young infants with clinical severe infection or critical illness, referral to a hospital remains the standard of care. If referral is not accepted, outpatient management with simplified antibiotic regimens is recommended. Two options are available: (1) oral amoxicillin twice daily for seven days plus injectable gentamicin once daily for seven days, or (2) oral amoxicillin twice daily for seven days plus injectable gentamicin once daily for two days. Both regimens have shown similar outcomes, and the choice depends on the health system's capacity to provide injectable antibiotics for seven versus two days. Follow-up care is essential for infants receiving outpatient treatment. Daily follow-up is recommended for those receiving seven days of gentamicin injections, while infants receiving two injections should be followed up on days two and four. National health strategies must integrate these guidelines into a continuum of care across all levels of the health system, consistent with the Every Newborn Action Plan. To implement the guideline effectively, countries must adapt the recommendations to their local contexts, strengthen referral mechanisms, improve the quality and accessibility of care, and invest in supportive supervision, monitoring, and evaluation. Additionally, research is needed to optimize the scale-up and management of PSBI in young infants when referral care is not accessible.
